title: My game reads any typed spell in 2 ms, offline, without an LLM. Here's how, and everything else AI did in it
author: Alarming_Shape_7144
selftext:
Hi! I'm a solo dev, and Magemind is my first paid game: a pixel-art castle defense where you type (or say) any spell, like "turn the ogres into chickens" or "summon a war tank", and the wizard casts it. Since this sub cares about how AI is actually used, here's the honest breakdown.

**Where AI was used**

Almost all of the code (Godot 4.7, GDScript) was written with Claude Code. I direct, design, test and make the calls; Claude writes and fixes. The project keeps a long CLAUDE.md with my rules and known engine pitfalls, and test scenarios run the real game and save screenshots, so it checks the result instead of guessing.

The translations into 6 languages were made with AI help. Music, many sound effects and the trailer narration come from ElevenLabs. The rest of the sound effects are synthesized from code.

**Where it wasn't**

The pixel art isn't from an image model. Every sprite sheet is painted pixel by pixel by GDScript tools with a fixed palette. A nice side effect: changing a sprite means editing code, so the art can evolve with the game.

**How the game understands spells**

This is the part I'm proudest of. By default there's no LLM involved. A sentence goes through two small local pieces.

The first is a keyword grimoire: hand-written rules in several languages. "Rain of fire" is fire, not water. "Freeze the wolf" makes the wolf the target, not a summon. It also reads counts, colors and creature traits.

The second is a tiny classifier embedded in the game, fastText-style. The sentence is split into words, word pairs and 3 to 5 letter chunks, which are hashed into 131k buckets. The average of those vectors goes through one hidden layer and then into separate outputs, one per field: spell shape, element, creature, building, effect, range, target, size, which animal to turn enemies into, and "is this even a spell?". It's 9 MB (int8), loads in about 4 ms and runs in about 1.4 ms in plain GDScript, doing exactly the same math as the Python training code.

The rules decide when they find something clear. The classifier decides when they find nothing or only a weak hint, and that's where it shines: synonyms ("fry these goblins"), typos ("fierball"), voice mistakes ("idra" for hydra), slang, and sentences that aren't spells at all.

It was trained on 240k synthetic sentences generated from vocabulary lists, with typos and speech errors mixed in (the training code was written with Claude Code too). On a hard test set I wrote before training, 254 sentences with synonyms, typos and slang in 6 languages, the rules alone got 145 right. Rules plus classifier get 250. With words it never saw in training, it still picks the right spell shape 92% of the time.

What comes out is a recipe: one of 108 spell shapes, plus element, creature, count, colors and effect. The game, not the model, sets damage and mana from fixed rules, with hard caps: power 1 to 5, at most 12 projectiles or creatures, speed bonus at most 1.6x. Type "kill all the monsters" and the wizard gives it a try and faints. Nothing you type can break the balance.

Earlier versions used a local LLM (Qwen3 on llama.cpp). It understood well, but every spell took seconds and it needed a 5 to 18 GB download. The classifier replaced it and casting became instant.

**The optional LLM**

If you paste your own OpenAI key, a GPT model fills that same recipe through a strict JSON schema, with a spell name and a one-line description. Same caps, same damage rules, and any error falls back to the local path. Voice mode runs whisper.cpp on your own machine (Windows only for now).

Free demo, first 5 waves, Windows and Linux: https://poweredie.itch.io/magemind

Happy to answer questions about the classifier, the code-drawn art, or building a full game with Claude Code.

comments.author: bluesmaker
comments.body:
This looks pretty cool. 

I do wonder about the limits of "if you can type it the wizard will cast it." 

What would it do if you say "Summon Superman"? 

What about NSFW things? Like "Summon a massive penis that shoots fire!"

Gameplay wise, is there a reason to change spells? Like are some enemies weaker to certain elements? Or some enemies that come in dense packs so AoE is important? Maybe I overlooked it, but the ad you made doesn't seem to tell how there is strategy to spell choice.

replies.author: Alarming_Shape_7144
replies.body:
Thanks! Great questions.

Right now there are no specific animations for those, so the game just falls back to the closest thing it understands.

That's actually where I want to take it. The plan is to keep adding absurd spells and summons with their own art (there are already things like dropping a fridge on an ogre, or a war tank), and for stuff that doesn't make sense in the game, NSFW included, have the wizard react instead of just failing. A comic moment, a disappointed look, or a little punishment. It already works that way for impossible requests: if you type "kill all the monsters", the wizard tries way too hard, a hurricane or lightning goes off, and he faints for a moment while the horde keeps walking.

On strategy, you're right that the trailer doesn't show it well. Every enemy has elemental weaknesses and resistances (you can click one to inspect it), and repeating the same element loses power unless it's what they're weak to. Elements also react with each other, so freezing and then shattering, or soaking with water and then using lightning, hits much harder. Ground spells don't reach flyers, dense packs reward area spells, and every fifth wave a boss shows up with its own weaknesses. So the fun is in what you write, but what you choose to write still matters a lot.

replies.author: bluesmaker
replies.body: Ah, cool. Glad to hear you're wanting to accommodate absurd spells. The strategy stuff sounds engaging. If you end up making another ad at some point, you should consider emphasizing that stuff more. I think the creative spells + strategy sells the idea more. GL!

comments.author: baz1nga007
comments.body: interesting way to doing that without LLm

comments.author: Azilen
comments.body: Remember me of Scribblenauts, it had the same concept of 'create anything you type' way before the LLMs existed. The problem of that game is that you could beat anything by typing 'invincible superman'', 'Cthulhu' and it would take all the difficulty away. How are you limiting the player to avoid them using only the most OP thing imaginable?

replies.author: Alarming_Shape_7144
replies.body: Scribblenauts was a big inspiration, and that was one of the first problems I had to solve. What you type only decides how the spell looks and behaves, never how strong it is. The idea is that everything depends on the wizard's mana, and mana has a limit. The game sets the power on a 1 to 5 scale, bigger spells cost more, and summons are capped in number and duration. So if you call something that's truly immortal or godlike, the wizard either brings a toned-down version of it that he can actually afford, or he overloads trying to create it and faints, with a funny animation and a real penalty while the horde keeps walking. That already happens if you try something like "kill all the monsters".

comments.author: PurchaseCommercial34
comments.body:
Curious how the rules + classifier merge works per field. If the grimoire is sure about the element ("fire") but finds nothing for shape or target, does the classifier only fill the empty fields, or does it redo the whole recipe? Since each head predicts on its own, filling field by field could give you combos the model would never pick together.  
  
Also wondering if the demo logs the sentences that fall through to the classifier with low confidence. Real players are going to type stuff your vocabulary lists never generated, and that seems like the best source for the next hard test set.

replies.author: Alarming_Shape_7144
replies.body:
It's field by field, never the whole recipe, and each field has its own threshold. For the element, a clear element word from the rules stays. The classifier takes over when the rules found nothing or only a weak hint, and rarely when the model is near certain and gives the rules' pick almost zero chance. The shape works the same way with three levels of evidence: none, a common word list, or a strong keyword. The stronger the rules' evidence, the higher the bar for the model. Quantity, colors, creature traits and building sturdiness always come from the rules.

On combos the model would never pick together: the heads share one embedding and one hidden layer, so they aren't fully independent, but your point stands. I handle it with constraints and tests. A summon only counts with a creature, a building only with a structure type, and a creature right after "on/at/against" is treated as a target. There's also a coherence test over 4,000 generated spells that flags things like a summon with no creature. Beyond that, an unusual combo is still a valid spell, because the game computes damage and mana from the recipe either way.

On logging: no, nothing is logged or sent anywhere, it all runs offline. I agree it would be the best source for the next hard set. If I add it, it would be an opt-in local file the player can choose to share, not silent telemetry. For now, phrases people post in threads like this one already end up as test cases.
